title: Ahead of ICJ genocide ruling on 19 November, minister presses UN envoy on Rohingya returns
excerpt: Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told UN Special Rapporteur Kelley Currie that more than 1.5 million Rohingya live in Bangladesh, above official records.

image.alt: Rows of bamboo and tarpaulin shelters in Kutupalong refugee camp, Cox's Bazar
image.credit: John Owens (VOA) / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

content:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed met Kelley E Currie, the UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, at the Secretariat in Dhaka on Wednesday, 11 November, The Observer Bangladesh reported. The meeting came eight days before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) gives its judgment in the genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar.

What the minister raised

  • Safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation, which he called the “primary objective” of international efforts.
  • His estimate that more than 1.5 million Rohingya are living in Bangladesh, above the number in official records, and the “significant burden” on the economy.
  • Law and order in the camps, and help with training and technology to tackle drug trafficking, arms smuggling and cybercrime.
  • Coordinated diplomatic pressure on Myanmar from China, India, the United States and the European Union, and a responsible role for the international community around the ICJ verdict.

Currie praised the government for the shelter and services it provides to Rohingya refugees, the report said. The minister’s 1.5 million figure is his own estimate; Aid agencies, including Oxfam, put the refugee population at nearly 1.2 million.

The ICJ judgment

The ICJ will deliver its judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar on 19 November, Human Rights Watch said. The Gambia filed the case in November 2019, arguing that Myanmar’s 2017 military operations in northern Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh, breached the Genocide Convention. The case concerns Myanmar’s responsibility as a state, not individual criminal guilt. The judgment is final and cannot be appealed.

“The International Court of Justice’s Myanmar judgment will mark a crucial moment in the Rohingya’s quest for justice,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.

Why it matters

A ruling against Myanmar would add legal and diplomatic weight to calls for accountability and safe return, though the court cannot enforce repatriation itself. For agencies in Cox’s Bazar, the days around the verdict may bring gatherings and heightened tension in the camps, as the minister’s focus on security suggests. Donors facing a smaller and underfunded 2026 appeal will also be watching whether the ruling brings new political attention and money.

What to watch

  • The judgment on 19 November and the responses of Bangladesh, Myanmar and ASEAN.
  • Camp security arrangements and community messaging around the verdict.
